name: Proof of Work
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Paying in Electricity: How Proof of Work Buys Trust
lesson.summary: Proof of work is a consensus mechanism that makes producing a valid block expensive and slow, while making it cheap and fast for everyone else to check, which is what makes rewriting history costly.
lesson.body:
Proof of work answers the consensus problem with a blunt but effective idea: make agreement expensive to fake. Instead of trusting a name or a vote count, which can be manufactured cheaply, the network only accepts a block if its header hash, produced by repeatedly trying different nonce values as described in the Nonce chapter, falls below a target that is deliberately hard to hit. Finding a value like that requires real computation, real electricity, and real time. Verifying it once found takes a single hash calculation, essentially instant by comparison.

That asymmetry, hard to produce, trivial to check, is the entire security argument. Anyone can look at a block's header, hash it once, and confirm the result meets the target, so no one has to trust the miner who found it. But producing a fake alternate history of many blocks in a row would require redoing all of that expensive work faster than the rest of the honest network is doing real work, which grows harder the further back an attacker tries to rewrite, since every subsequent block adds more cumulative cost on top. This is the practical reason a well established proof of work chain becomes harder to tamper with as more blocks are added on top of a given transaction.

The difficulty target is not fixed forever. Bitcoin, the best known example, recalculates its target every two thousand and sixteen blocks, roughly every two weeks given its ten minute average block time, comparing how long that batch of blocks actually took to produce against the ten minute goal, and adjusting the target up or down accordingly. If more miners join and blocks start coming faster than expected, the target tightens and mining gets harder. If miners leave and blocks slow down, the target loosens. This keeps block production roughly steady regardless of how much total computing power is pointed at the network at any given moment.

A simple way to picture the incentive is a locked box that only opens if you happen to guess the right combination out of billions of possibilities, and whoever opens it first gets to add the next page to the shared book and collect a reward for doing so. Everyone is trying combinations simultaneously, spending real electricity on every guess, and the winner's page is instantly checkable by everyone else with almost no effort. That is the whole mechanism, dressed up in cryptography rather than a physical lock.

Because this book is meant to be skeptical as well as accurate, it is worth naming the real cost directly: proof of work consumes genuine electricity at meaningful scale, since security here comes specifically from spending real world resources rather than from cleverness alone. Whether that cost is worth the tamper resistance it buys is a legitimate debate, and it is exactly why alternative consensus mechanisms, covered in later chapters, exist and have gained ground in parts of the industry.
